item.title: Russell Brand takes the stand at his rape and sexual assault trial
item.description:
Actor and comedian Russell Brand took the stand in his trial on rape and sexual assault charges in London on Wednesday.
Brand, 51, is accused of three counts of rape, three counts of sexual assault and one charge of attempted indecent assault.
The allegations, made by six female complainants, span a 10-year period between 1999 and 2009. Brand has pleaded not guilty to the charges.
He started the morning by answering questions on whether he committed each respective charge with a terse "no." Under cross-examination, he said he was innocent.
"My entire life has been consumed by these allegations," Brand said in his initial questioning. Under cross-examination, he said that while he believes he behaved promiscuously during the time period in question, he thinks that "consent is absolutely non-negotiable."
Russell Brand and wife Laura Brand arrive at court ahead of his trial, at Southwark Crown Court on October 28, 2026.
Alberto Pezzali / Getty Images
Brand calls consent "more important than sex itself"
One woman alleged she met Brand at a Labour Party conference in 1999. She believed Brand was gay, and invited him to her hotel room to continue a conversation that began after a cabaret show where he performed. She alleged he came out of the bathroom topless before raping her.
Brand said he remembers meeting the victim and chatting with her. When asked if he portrayed himself as gay, he said, "I don't think so." Brand said the victim was the one who suggested returning to her hotel room.
Brand said he believes he would have checked in with the woman during the encounter, and denied raping her. He said he believes "consent is fundamental, essential, necessary, and in many ways, more important than sex itself."

item.title: No clear winner in Israeli election as polls suggest stalemate
item.description:
No clear winner emerged in Israel's elections on Wednesday with the vote count still under way. Neither Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's coalition nor the opposition bloc, led by Gadi Eisenkot, secured a majority, according to exit polls on Tuesday night.
With 85% of votes counted, Netanyahu's Likud party has 20.8% and Eisenkot's Yashar party has 16.1%, according to official election data.
Local media projected 53 seats for Likud and allied parties, 48 for Yashar and allied parties and 19 for Arab-led parties. Each would need 61 seats for a majority in Israel's 120-seat parliament, known as the Knesset, in order to form a government.
On Wednesday morning, the head of Israel's main left-wing party called for his opposition allies to work with Arab parties to unseat Netanyahu.
"We must no longer accept Netanyahu's racist division between Jewish votes and Arab votes," Yair Golan said on X. "We have a responsibility. And we have an opportunity to form a government of change in partnership with Israel's Arab citizens."
Netanyahu dismissed the idea of partnership with Arab parties, instead calling on his allies to form a "right-wing, nationalist government."
"We must not endanger Israel and establish a government that relies on anti-Zionist Arab parties," Netanyahu said on Wednesday morning.
Israel's two Arab parties won more seats in parliament than in any previous election. That electoral success comes after what some Arab voters told CBS News was a difficult time for them in the country under the hard-right government of Netanyahu, prompting a historic turnout for the minority community.
Both Netanyahu and those opposing him have previously vowed not to form a government reliant on Arab parties, arguing it would endanger the country if they gain enough seats to influence Israel's engagement in its myriad conflicts. Arab citizens of Israel are around 20% of the population.

item.title: Flávio Bolsonaro leaves Brazil, lands in U.S. after election loss
item.description:
Brazilian Senator Flávio Bolsonaro and his family left the country on Tuesday after he lost Brazil's hotly contested presidential election over the weekend, and CBS News Miami reports they landed in Miami Wednesday morning.
Earlier, a senior State Department official told CBS News that Bolsonaro and his family would receive U.S. visas.
En route to the U.S., Bolsonaro, his wife and two daughters arrived in Argentina Tuesday night and hen boarded a private plane for a flight to Guayaquil, Ecuador, according to Argentinian officials and flight tracking data.
Bolsonaro, an ally of President Trump, departed Brazil for the U.S. after being defeated by incumbent President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva in Sunday's election.
A spokesperson for Bolsonaro did not respond to a request for comment. His campaign manager Rogério Marinho also refused to comment.
Silva said Tuesday it was "shameful" that Bolsonaro had fled Brazil.
"A person who sneaks out of their country must have something to hide," Silva said, per Agence France-Presse. "The act of leaving Brazil is shameful."
Bolsonaro's brother, Eduardo Bolsonaro, who lives in Texas, had publicly encouraged him to leave Brazil if he lost the election.
Bolsonaro has touted his relationship with Mr. Trump and visited the White House in May. The family connections go deeper: Brother Eduardo Bolsonaro was convicted in absentia in June of illegally lobbying the Trump administration and sentenced to four years in prison. A warrant was recently issued for his arrest.
Mr. Trump did not offer a full-throated endorsement of Bolsonaro in the runoff against Lula, as he has with some other right-of-center candidates in Latin America. But he suggested on Monday, without providing evidence, that Brazil's election was "rigged."

item.title: At least 64 reported dead in high-speed train crash in Spain
item.description:
A high-speed train reportedly slammed into the rear of another train that had stopped in central Spain, derailing two cars and killing at least 64 people Wednesday morning, according to local authorities.
The regional government of Castilla-La Mancha told the Reuters news agency the death toll had risen to 64. Earlier in the day, 80 people were reported injured.
The crash occurred Wednesday morning in the province of Toledo, according to Spain's rail system operator ADIF. Rail service was suspended between Madrid, Ciudad Real and Andalusia.
Emergency services attend to the victims at the scene of a collision between two trains in Urda, Spain, on Wednesday, Oct. 28, 2026.
Juanma Jiménez/AP
Padilla told state broadcaster TVE that the accident was between two high-speed trains heading in the same direction from Madrid to Seville and that one ran into the tail of the other while it was stopped, knocking two of its cars off the track. She said the cause of the crash was not known.
The accident involved a train from Spain's state-owned RENFE company and the private rail company IRYO. Trains from those two companies were also involved in a deadly crash in January.
Padilla said 397 passengers were in the RENFE train and 147 passengers were in the IRYO train.

item.title: U.S. cruise ship suspends around-the-world voyage due to fuel costs
item.description:
Sihanoukville, Cambodia — A U.S. cruise ship on an around-the-world voyage that touted its cabins as floating homes suspended its three-year voyage in Cambodia due to fuel costs, forcing hundreds of passengers to disembark.
The MV Odyssey set sail two years ago on a voyage to the seven continents marketed as combining long-term living at sea with global travel. Its operator had offered to "make the Odyssey your permanent home," with the purchase price of a suite for the lifetime of the vessel starting at around $230,000.
For now, it is docked at the Cambodian port of Sihanoukville on the Gulf of Thailand, with no certain departure date.
The MV Odyssey, a U.S. cruise ship, is seen docked at the Sihanoukville Autonomous Port in Sihanoukville, Cambodia, on Oct. 28, 2026.
AP Photo / Heng Sinith
The ship has been carrying 203 passengers, mostly Americans, along with 156 crew members, according to Cambodian officials. It has a 650-passenger capacity.
Its Florida-based operator, Villa Vie Residences, said monthly fuel expenses per cabin that historically averaged $1,800 have reached an estimated $6,000 to $8,000 in parts of Asia due to the war in Iran. The company said it sought to reduce fuel consumption by slowing the itinerary and spending more time in port, but was unable to offset the surging costs.
Traffic has been curtailed in the Strait of Hormuz since the war in Iran began, squeezing supplies of all kinds of petroleum-based fuels, especially in Southeast Asia, and sharply increasing prices.
The average price for a gallon of diesel fuel the day before the war started, Feb. 27, 2026, was $3.76, according to AAA, and was $6.52 late last month, an increase of $2.76.

item.description:

item.title: Iran war has cost $47 billion, U.S. military says
item.description:
The war with Iran has cost the U.S. military at least $47.1 billion as of mid-October, according to a new estimate from U.S. Central Command obtained by CBS News.
The bulk of the war's price tag is the cost of replacing expended munitions, which CENTCOM pegged at around $29 billion, according to the latest estimate, which was provided to lawmakers. The military also tallied $6.1 billion to replace lost equipment and around $11.9 billion in incremental costs like support for American service members.
The estimate does not include the cost of damage to U.S. military bases in the Middle East, many of which were targeted by Iranian drones and missiles.
By comparison, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth told lawmakers three months ago the war had cost around $37.5 billion, not including damaged U.S. bases.
The Congressional Budget Office said last month the war could cost $2 billion to $3 billion per month for as long as it continues, in part due to the need to replace interceptor missiles to defend against Iranian attacks. That cost could rise during tit-for-tat exchanges between the U.S. and Iran, which were common over the summer but have been quiet in recent weeks.
CBS News has reached out to the Pentagon for comment.
The Iran war will enter its ninth month this week, and the conflict's future is unclear. President Trump has suggested he might restart hostilities with Iran after next month's midterm elections unless Iran agrees to a deal. "We may do another little Epic Fury, or they'll agree," he told supporters during a rally in Florida last week.
The Pentagon's inspector general said last month the U.S. is facing "strategic inventory shortfalls" due to the number of munitions expended during the war, leading the Defense Department to work to speed up production.
